questions.q: What does Salesforce's EDA (Education Data Architecture) provide that this design builds on, rather than reinventing?
options: A complete replacement for the Student Information System
A dedicated object model only for financial aid processing
A pre-built foundation of affiliations, relationships, courses, and terms extending standard objects, already modeling how people relate to the institution and each other
A standalone mobile app with no connection to the standard Salesforce object model
questions.explain: EDA extends standard Account/Contact objects with affiliation and relationship modeling built for exactly this kind of institution-and-person relationship, which is why the advising design should sit on top of it rather than duplicating it.

questions.q: Why does FERPA push this design toward a default of less access rather than the broader-by-default visibility common in many enterprise CRM designs?
options: Because FERPA restricts access to student education records to those with a legitimate educational interest, so an advisor should see only their own assigned students by default
Because FERPA requires every record in the org to be fully public
Because FERPA only applies to financial data, not advising notes
Because FERPA bans the use of private organization-wide defaults
questions.explain: FERPA's legitimate-educational-interest standard is the reason the sharing model starts private and grants access narrowly through the advisor-assignment relationship, rather than starting broad.

questions.q: What makes guardian access to a student's advising record a textbook case of consent-driven sharing?
options: Guardians automatically receive full access the moment a student enrolls
Guardian access is controlled entirely by the university's registrar with no student input
Consent, once granted, can never be revoked under this design
Access is granted only after the student explicitly names the guardian and grants consent, which is itself an auditable, revocable record
questions.explain: The defining feature of consent-driven sharing here is that access is conditional on an explicit, checkable, revocable grant by the student — not a role-based or family-relationship default.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce receive enrollment status and course load from the SIS through an integration, rather than becoming the authoritative source for that data itself?
options: Because Salesforce is technically incapable of storing enrollment data
Because the SIS stays the system of record for official academic data, and duplicating that authority in Salesforce risks creating a second, out-of-sync version of the truth
Because FERPA specifically forbids CRM systems from ever touching enrollment data
Because the advising case study does not need any enrollment information at all
questions.explain: This repeats the system-of-record / system-of-engagement split seen elsewhere in this chapter: Salesforce supports the advising relationship without trying to become a second authoritative academic record.

questions.q: A student revokes a guardian's consent to view their advising notes. What must actually happen for this to be a defensible design, not just a cosmetic change?
options: The guardian's actual access to the advising record must be removed the moment consent is revoked, driven by the same mechanism that granted it in the first place
The consent field is marked "revoked" but the guardian's Experience Cloud access is left unchanged until the next scheduled data cleanup
The student must contact IT to manually delete the guardian's user account
Revocation only applies to future advising notes, not notes the guardian already viewed
questions.explain: A revocable consent record that doesn't actually remove access when revoked isn't a real control — the sharing mechanism granting guardian access has to be tied directly to the live state of the consent record.
